articles.title: Ranking the Democratic 2028 presidential contenders
articles.summary: Democrats are already looking beyond November’s midterms to the 2028 presidential contest — and they like what they see. For now, Republicans are weighed down by President Trump’s low approval ratings and broader voter concerns about the economy. Democrats guess whoever becomes the GOP nominee in 2028 will suffer from the president’s liabilities without being…
articles.body:
Democrats are already looking beyond November’s midterms to the 2028 presidential contest — and they like what they see.

For now, Republicans are weighed down by President Trump’s low approval ratings and broader voter concerns about the economy.

Democrats guess whoever becomes the GOP nominee in 2028 will suffer from the president’s liabilities without being able to replicate his visceral connection to the MAGA base.

There is no runaway contender for the Democratic nomination, however. That’s a factor encouraging numerous potential contenders to think about a run.

It could be a large field in 2028, and there are a number of credible candidates who could top any list of contenders at this early stage.

The notion of a successful bid for the nomination from Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) becomes more real by the day.

Ideological opponents often disparage the chances of a 36-year-old, leftist Latina from New York becoming a winning candidate nationwide.

But that underestimates the panoply of political strengths that AOC, as she is widely known, brings.

She is far and away the most charismatic candidate of the left, which is enjoying a surge of momentum within the Democratic Party.

Her capacity to connect with voters in unusual ways has been shown yet again in recent weeks, especially through her regular video updates about her decision to begin freezing her eggs.

Ocasio-Cortez, a far more astute strategist than she is often given credit for, is plainly positioning herself for a bid.

Her blithe dismissal of “woke 1” as “crazy” during an ABC News interview last month seemed designed to inoculate her from criticism about the perceived excesses of that agenda.

She is shaking up her team , with the departure of her longtime campaign manager.

And even small habits, like her propensity to take random on-camera questions from reporters as she walks near the steps of the Capitol, keep her central to the conversation.

It’s still quite possible that Ocasio-Cortez chooses to stay in the House or challenges Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) in a primary rather than seek the White House.

But if she runs, it will be a real struggle for anyone to beat her in a Democratic primary.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom is Ocasio-Cortez’s most obvious competitor for front-runner status.

The governor of the nation’s most populous state has been open about his interest in seeking the top office.

He has battled Trump both in public remarks and in regular jabs on social media.

On a more substantive level, California has been in the vanguard of attempts by Democratic states to stymie Trump’s agenda in the courts.

Newsom also appears to be doing his best to shake off the idea that he is a “coastal elite” figure who is ill-equipped to connect with a broader public.

He is on a tour of Southern states this week. A memoir earlier this year saw him write about his early troubles with dyslexia and an upbringing that was split between a wealthy father and a mother who struggled financially.

The California governor would have no problem raising the money to support a presidential bid.

There are, to be sure, enduring concerns about Newsom’s ability to win in the heartlands.

But right now, he and Ocasio-Cortez feel like they have a jump on the rest of the field.

Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) is the breakout star of this midterm cycle for Democrats.

He was once thought to be in real danger of losing his reelection fight in Georgia, a state that Trump won in 2024.

Instead, Ossoff is now a strong favorite over GOP challenger Rep. Mike Collins (Ga.). The last two major polls of the race have put him up by 8 points and 9 points.

But it’s not only Ossoff’s chances of reelection that commend him to Democrats.

He has become a national star in part because of slickly filmed campaign videos that have often gone viral. Fans see tonal echoes of former President Obama in the senator’s penchant for rhetoric that is simultaneously elevated and pugnacious.

A recent reference to White House aide Natalie Harp and her closeness to Trump was controversial in some quarters but delighted the most fervent members of the Democratic base.

Skeptics argue that Ossoff’s appeal is too reliant on slick packaging and wonder how he would stand up to the intense spotlight of a presidential campaign.

But there’s no question that he would be a serious contender if he ran.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris is in an odd spot.

The trauma Democrats feel about her loss to Trump in 2024 may militate against them nominating her again. Her argument — in essence, that her campaign did not have enough time after then-President Biden dramatically dropped out of the race — is questionable at best.

Still, Harris leads almost every early poll of the 2028 field. Is that simply a function of name recognition, as her detractors would say, or evidence that she is held in higher regard by actual Democratic voters than she is among the pundit class?

This past week, Harris was measured about Democratic midterm candidates in competitive races who seemingly want to keep their distance from her.

She said in a phone interview with MS NOW that she would campaign where “helpful” but was also understanding about candidates “doing whatever they need to do to win.”

Harris has another big asset. She is already a history-making figure, as the first Black woman and first person of South Asian heritage to be either vice president or the nominee of a major party.

If she runs again, she would start with real strength among Black voters, who are critical in any Democratic contest.

It doesn’t hurt her chances that the first primary will be in South Carolina, either.

5. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg

Former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg outperformed expectations back in the 2020 primaries, especially for someone whose only office at that time was as the former Mayor of South Bend, Ind.

Buttigieg, a graduate of Harvard and a former Rhodes scholar who speaks eight languages, has intellectual firepower to burn. He often puts it to use in interviews with media outlets that are not known to be friendly toward Democrats.

But there can sometimes be questions around what Buttigieg’s core beliefs actually are. He also struggled badly with Black voters in 2020, which is a weakness that would need to be remedied if he is to have any real shot at the nomination.

llinois Gov. JB Pritzker has emerged as one of the most aggressive critics of Trump among front-line Democrats.

Earlier this week, this approach even found expression in opposition to Trump traveling to Illinois for a golf tournament later this month.

“He is neither wanted here nor needed here,” Pritzker said in a statement, which also asserted that if Trump insisted on coming he should “explain to Illinoisans why his tariffs have made groceries, electricity, and everything else too damned expensive.”

The billionaire Pritzker would have no problem self-funding a campaign. He has all the toughness for which Chicago politics is legendary.

The question is how he can outflank the people higher on this list.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s appeal is fairly obvious. He is a popular governor of a state that is crucial in the Electoral College. He is expected to coast to reelection in November, leading by double-digits in some polls.

The governor’s appeal in Pennsylvania could plausibly be replicated in other battlegrounds deeper into the Midwest, notably Wisconsin and Michigan.

Shapiro would be well-positioned to try to secure the support of more centrist Democrats. His political identity stands in clear contrast to the more progressive wing.

That being said, this same dynamic has its downside — especially with regard to Israel.

Shapiro’s 2024 comparison of pro-Palestinian demonstrators to the Ku Klux Klan still rankles the left.

More broadly, the vigor of his support for Israel looks increasingly incongruous in a party that has come to view the issue of Israel, Gaza and the Palestinians as a kind of moral litmus test.

Much of the conjecture around 2028 Democrats is premised on the idea that Ocasio-Cortez is more likely to run than not.

If she takes a pass, a lot changes. More running room would immediately open up for other candidates on the left.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who said last month he is “kicking the tires” on a 2028 campaign, could be a bigger beneficiary than some other leftist contenders such as Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).

Van Hollen arguably has greater mainstream appeal and is less identified with the harder edges of the left. At the same time, he has real appeal to progressives.

The Maryland senator’s potential appeal was summed up in a recent remark on NBC’s “Meet the Press,” when he said he would not reject an endorsement from people connected to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) but swiftly added , “but I’m certainly not seeking the endorsement from the DSA.”

Rahm Emanuel has been hitting the media trail hard in recent months.

In the process, he has lamented that his party’s brand has become “toxic” and is seen by too many voters as “weak” and “woke.”

He says Democrats need to spend less time talking about “bathrooms and locker rooms” — in other words, about the battle over trans rights.

That may or may not be true as a raw political calculation.

But it’s uncertain whether today’s Democratic Party wants someone as its standard-bearer who first became nationally prominent during the Clinton presidency — and who shares much of the 42nd president’s instinct for “third way” triangulation.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) is a very effective communicator, including on social media.

It’s possible that if Democrats wanted a nominee with the ability to speak to both the left and the center-left, he could be in with a shot.

This week, as he did his annual “walk across Connecticut,” he told The Washington Post that Democrats need to be “telling the true story about the way that the economy is losing to benefit the very, very rich and the corporations.”

Murphy would face real challenges in picking his way through a crowded field to become a real contender, however.

Also in the mix: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Sen. Cory Booker (N.J.), Sen. Mark Kelly (Ariz.) and Rep. Ro Khanna (Calif.). Two Democratic governors who have indicated they will not run — Wes Moore of Maryland and Gretchen Whitmer of Michigan — would be plausible candidates if they reconsidered.

articles.title: Abdul El-Sayed hits back at Israel questions, suggests his name and faith are behind press scrutiny
articles.summary: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed suggested reporters press him on the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and faith.
articles.body: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed suggested that reporters press him about the Israel-Hamas war because of his name and his faith. Speaking on Detroit Public Radio’s "MichMash" podcast, El-Sayed pushed back on host Zach Gorchow’s line of questioning about the Israel-Hamas conflict, suggesting that his name and Muslim faith play a role in the media attention surrounding the issue. "You've been asked many times whether you support a two-state solution regarding the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and you generally say you support equal rights to self-determination for Jewish Israelis and Palestinians," Gorchow said. "Can you tell us, what does that mean?" MICHIGAN DEM HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED JABS CNN GIVING HIM 'NON-CONSENSUAL COLONOSCOPY' IN RECENT INTERVIEWS "Zach, with all due respect, this has been hashed and rehashed," El-Sayed began. "This is the MichMash podcast. I'm focused on what's happening for the 10 million people in this state." El-Sayed then suggested the media’s interest in his stance on the conflict was related to his identity. MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE CONFRONTED REPEATEDLY OVER ISRAEL’S RIGHT TO EXIST, DEFUNDING THE POLICE "It's so frustrating to me that people want to make this race about something that's happening 6,000 miles away, when we've got kids who can't afford a next meal here at home," he continued. The controversial candidate went on to blast the constant line of questioning from members of the press regarding his stance on providing aid to Israel — a topic he has remained staunchly against throughout his campaign. MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL CALLS AIPAC DONATIONS 'LEGALIZED BRIBERY,' REMAINS SILENT ON OTHER DONATIONS "I just find it so interesting that I never get asked about this question on the stump," El-Sayed told the host. "But it seems to me that every time I sit down with anybody in the press, it seems that that's the most important question." El-Sayed continued by suggesting the media’s focus on his stance on Israel could be related to his name and Muslim faith. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS "It tends to be the first question everybody likes to ask me," he said. "I wonder why? I mean, does it have something to do with my name? Maybe, you know, how I pray?" He concluded by doubling-down on his assertion that his campaign is focused on the people of Michigan — not the people of Israel. MICHIGAN DEMOCRATIC SENATE CANDIDATE CLAIMS ISRAEL 'JUST AS EVIL' AS HAMAS "It's fascinating to me that I'm running to represent ten million people who live here, and you want to ask about people living somewhere else," El-Sayed continued. "And I just think I want to be talking about [the] people living here." According to data compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, Michigan is home to 129,225 Jewish residents — which comprise roughly 1.3% of the state’s population. JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE El-Sayed’s comments were of interest to CEO of Axia Public Relations Jason Mudd, who told Fox News Digital his ability to flip the narrative on the press shows a level of message discipline. But when you listen to the full episode, he never uses the word racist. He questions why the topic keeps coming up and ties it to his name and his faith. He's pointing to bias." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If El-Sayed were my client, I'd advise him to name the bias claim directly instead of leaving it implied, then answer the follow-up on what his position actually means in the same breath. Right now the framing comes first, and he still hasn't answered the follow-up." Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

articles.title: Trump weighs in on Lindsay Clancy murder trial dubbed 'kangaroo court' by GOP leaders
articles.summary: Trump says Lindsay Clancy will pay "the price" after a mistrial was declared when the jury deadlocked 11-1 in the Massachusetts murder case.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said Lindsay Clancy will still have to pay "the price" for the deaths of her three small children — Cora 5, Dawson 3, and Callan, 8 months — after a mistrial was ruled on Friday. During a press gaggle in the Oval Office, a reporter asked Trump if he'd been following the murder trial of Clancy, a Massachusetts mom whose defense did not deny that she strangled her children with exercise bands in January 2023, but argued that she was not guilty by reason of insanity. Her attorneys claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis, a severe but rare psychiatric condition in which a person is disconnected from reality. "It's a horrible tragedy," Trump shared with reporters. "It's a horrible tragedy. I see what's happened, and it looks like it's a hung jury." "I assume there's going to be another trial. It's a terrible situation. Look, she did a horrible, horrible thing. Can't be worse. But you'll find out what the price to pay is. There'll be a price. It's going to be [a] mental institution or jail or something," Trump continued. LINDSAY CLANCY MISTRIAL DECLARED AFTER JURY DEADLOCKS IN KILLINGS OF HER THREE CHILDREN The six-week trial, which was supposed to determine whether Clancy was to be held criminally responsible, quickly evolved into a flashpoint in the internet culture war over women's postpartum mental health and spurred misinformation and conspiracy theories, including false claims accusing her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, of being responsible for the children’s deaths. After nearly a week of deliberations, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when the jury deadlocked 11 to 1: 11 jurors voted to acquit Clancy, while one holdout refused to join them. The jury consisted of 9 women and 3 men. PROSECUTOR IN INFAMOUS KILLER MOM CASE SAYS WOMEN ON LINDSAY CLANCY JURY MAY BRING ‘STRANGE TWIST’ TO VERDICT Clancy's defense attorney requested that the lone juror be removed because a note given to the judge by the jurors said the holdout had doubt but refused to apply it, according to People. The mistrial invoked a strong reaction from Republican lawmakers, while Democratic lawmakers and leaders — including those from Clancy's state — have remained mum on the high-profile case. "Out of 12 people, only ONE had the courage to hold a serial killer accountable for her actions," Rep. Michael Rulli, R-Ohio, posted on X. "That’s not just bravery. That’s a hero." "Holdout juror’s going to need security," Sen. Mike Lee, R-Ohio, posted on X. "Sad." Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis called the mistrial a "miscarriage of justice." "The victims deserved far, far better than a kangaroo court," DeSantis wrote. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., who has been incredibly vocal against Clancy's supporters — who have been gathered outside the courthouse and posted videos showing support online — suggesting Clancy would not have this support if she were Black. "This case is not about the excuses for why she committed murder," Mace posted on X. "This is about justice for the three beautiful souls whose lives were taken after their mother strangled them with her bare hands and workout bands." PATRICK CLANCY SPEAKS OUT AFTER HUNG JURY IN LINDSAY CLANCY CASE, ADDRESSES PROSPECT OF ANOTHER TRIAL "12 jurors looked at this onesie," Mace continued. "Only ONE stood his ground to defend the children." But Clancy's defense argued that she was a devoted and loving mother who was desperately seeking to get help, alleging that the cocktail of medications she was on worsened her mental state. Clancy had been prescribed 13 psychiatric medications — more than 30 prescriptions — in the four months leading up to the murders. Patrick Clancy is suing for wrongful death and medical malpractice against Clancy's providers, Dr. Jennifer Tufts, Rebecca Jollotta, Aster Mental Health and South Shore Health System. Clancy also filed a separate lawsuit alleging negligence, medical malpractice and personal injury. "Lindsay was struggling. We were all very concerned," Susan Clancy, Clancy's mother-in-law, told jurors. "She was very nurturing, very loving. She was a wonderful mother. Wonderful." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Clancy is due back in court Sept. 29 for a status hearing, trial assignment and a defense Rule 25 motion.

articles.title: The rise of the anti-social American
articles.summary: Writer John Mac Ghlionn argues that modern American life has shifted toward extreme isolation and digital dependency, sacrificing genuine human connection for technological convenience.
articles.body:
The American welcome mat used to mean something; now it’s just the designated drop-off zone for the Amazon courier. There was a time, not that long ago, when the average suburban street was full of unannounced drop-ins, the smell of burning charcoal, and scattered lawn chairs. Today, neighborhoods possess the lifeless feel of a well-maintained cemetery. The modern American Dream is best described as a private bunker where the outside world arrives entirely in a cardboard box or a fiber-optic cable.

Americans now spend considerably less time with other people than they did 20 years ago. This is a magnificent triumph of optimization. The human animal is notoriously unreliable. He’s prone to bad breath, political rants, and requests to help move heavy furniture. Eliminating the physical neighbor in favor of a digital stream is a sensible defense mechanism. The local bar , once a breeding ground for scandalous gossip and collective hangovers, has been soundly defeated by DoorDash and a high-definition TV. America has achieved the pinnacle of individual autonomy: the right to die alone in a perfectly temperature-controlled living room.

The modern economy operates on the premise that human contact is a design flaw. Up until the early 2000s, buying a loaf of bread required a verbal exchange with a cashier who might comment on the weather. Today, self-checkout kiosks and gig-economy couriers ensure that a citizen could survive for six consecutive months without uttering a single syllable to another member of the species. The delivery driver leaves the paper bag on the porch, rings the bell, and vanishes into the bushes like a timid woodland creature. This arrangement represents the peak of convenience, but at a cost so severe that it reduces human interaction to a transaction of mutual avoidance.

This structural shift toward complete insulation has naturally changed how Americans allocate their emotional resources. The supposedly outdated concept of friendship required actual physical stamina. It demanded driving across town, listening to tedious stories about a stranger’s root canal, and pretending to enjoy terrible homemade casserole. The digital landscape solved this problem by converting relationships into a currency of metrics. A person can now maintain five hundred “connections” from the comfort of a porcelain toilet seat. It’s now possible to receive a constant stream of validation without the exhausting requirement of showing up at a hospital bedside or helping someone paint their garage. It is an exquisite system of emotional capitalism in which everyone is an investor and no one performs the actual labor.

The logical conclusion of this optimization is as depressing as it is inevitable. Millions of citizens now spend their evenings conversing with large language models (LLMs), pouring their deepest fears into software that could ultimately use those vulnerabilities to destroy them. The machine is the perfect companion. It never interrupts, and it will never ask to borrow $50. It provides the illusion of intimacy without the terrifying risk of human rejection. A generation raised on the predictable feedback loops of video games has found its ultimate match: a partner that is literally programmed to agree with everything they say.

This reliance on artificial empathy reflects a broader cultural realization that human relationships are simply too taxing to maintain. Between skyrocketing rent and the sheer exhaustion of everyday life, a chatbot quickly becomes the easiest companion. The traditional pillars of community — the local church, the bowling league, the union hall — all required an investment of time, vulnerability and occasionally a membership fee. The algorithm requires only your eyeballs.

Even leisure activities have been thoroughly scrubbed of any genuine spontaneity. The casual afternoon stroll or the unrecorded vacation is an extinct concept. Every minute of non-work time must be weaponized for personal branding, tracked via GPS, or cataloged for public consumption. A meal is no longer a source of nutrition but a piece of content that must be styled, lit, and uploaded to prove to an indifferent audience that the consumer is alive and very much enjoying themselves. The act of living has become a corporate marketing campaign managed by a staff of one.

The ultimate casualty of this hyper-efficient lifestyle is the concept of unmonetized time. Spending three hours sitting on a porch talking about nothing is an economic absurdity in a culture that demands constant self-improvement and digital engagement. Americans, like much of modern society, are constantly connected to the world yet increasingly detached from the floorboards beneath their feet. The American experiment began with the pursuit of liberty and has culminated in the freedom to sit in an empty room, stare at a screen, and beg a box of wires for a digital pat on the head. America may still be the greatest nation on the planet, but it’s fast becoming a nation of strangers.

John Mac Ghlionn is a writer and researcher who explores culture, society and the impact of technology on daily life.

articles.title: Kennedy Center closes after ceiling piece falls: ‘President Trump has been right’
articles.summary: A portion of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer collapsed Friday evening as heavy rain swept through the Washington, D.C. area, prompting officials to temporarily close the main building. No one was injured in the collapse, according to the Kennedy Center, which released photos from the scene showing chunks of the ceiling and…
articles.body:
A portion of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s Grand Foyer collapsed Friday evening as heavy rain swept through the Washington, D.C. area, prompting officials to temporarily close the main building.

No one was injured in the collapse, according to the Kennedy Center, which released photos from the scene showing chunks of the ceiling and dust scattered across the foyer’s red carpet.

The Grand Foyer, a sprawling hallway connecting the Opera House, Concert Hall and Eisenhower Theater, will remain restricted to visitors and nonessential personnel through the week, according to internal communications obtained by ABC News. The rest of the main building is expected to reopen Saturday.

Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi pointed to the collapse as evidence of the need for extensive renovations at the performing arts complex in a statement to ABC.

She said the ceiling failure “stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership.”

The incident comes as the Kennedy Center is at the center of an ongoing legal fight over its Trump-appointed board’s plans for the building.

The board has approved closing the center for roughly two years for a sweeping renovation. Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), an ex-officio member of the board, has challenged the closure plan in federal court.

The dispute also involves efforts to recognize President Trump on the building. The board has sought to add language to the facade crediting Trump with the center’s renovation, a move Beatty is also challenging in court.

The Justice Department has argued that extensive work is necessary to address the building’s condition, citing problems with water damage and rusting steel.

The administration threatened to demolish the building if a judge were to block the center’s closure for repairs, and has repeatedly referred to the center as being in a “decrepit” condition in court filings.

articles.title: Bettors are harassing college athletes. It’s time for Congress to act.
articles.summary: As illegal sports betting continues to fuel online abuse against collegiate athletes, there is growing calls for Congress to pass federal legislation establishing a national banned bettors registry and allowing athletes to sue harassers.
articles.body:
Growing up, mom always said, “if you don’t have anything nice to say, then don’t say anything at all.” While she was unaware at the time, this phrase may become pointed legal advice — especially if you are a college sports fan or bettor.

College athletes across the country deal with abusive and vulgar messages from sports fans daily. Take Florida State forward Cam Corhen for example, who after being injured early in a basketball game and only scoring two points, returned to his phone filled with hateful messages from bettors, including one that said, “I hope your mom dies.” Or, North Carolina forward Armando Bacot, who received over one hundred messages demeaning him for having too few rebounds, just 12 days after North Carolina legalized player prop bets on collegiate sports.

Collegiate athlete harassment stemming from sports betting is a widespread issue. One in three high-profile athletes receive abusive messages from people with a betting interest. Student-athletes are demanded to strenuously prepare for their competitions multiple times per day, compete at a high level each week, and simultaneously, perform well academically. Beyond that, in the age of NIL , they are incentivized for maintaining extremely public-facing profiles online. These athletes face an impossible choice: build the public profile NIL demands or protect themselves from relentless online abuse.

Because these young athletes should not have to make such a decision at this stage in their lives, federal legislation is necessary to combat the issue. As legalized sports betting intensifies fan motivation to abusively target athletes, Congress must intervene by implementing a national banned bettors registry for individuals convicted of sports-related harassment and by allowing athletes to sue people who engage in repeated betting related harassment.

Now, it is easier than ever to place bets on individual players via prop bets that allow bettors to place wagers on specific player statistics. This gives fans greater cause to direct their harassment toward individual athletes. Some advocates even argue in favor of banning prop bets on college athletics or eliminating college sports betting altogether. However, because those courses of action are guaranteed to be met with fierce opposition advocacy by the gambling lobby and will take much longer to implement, federal legislation is a better, more expedient option.

This issue has not gone unnoticed, but the measures in place to deter or cure online abuse are failing. Social media or culture campaigns like the NCAA’s “Don’t Be a Loser” initiative encourage fans to be mindful of the statistics underlying gambling related harassment of student-athletes, but awareness campaigns lack teeth.

Additionally, the current legal framework underlying this issue is highly decentralized. Some states ban prop bets and others do not . Some implement banned bettor lists, and some prohibit all sports betting. This structure makes it impossible to protect all collegiate athletes across state lines.

To address this gap, Congress should implement a federal standard that targets online harassment tied to sports betting. First, federal legislation should impose criminal penalties for individuals who engage in online conduct that causes substantial emotional distress or fear for safety. A model for this approach can be found in a New York’s Senate Bill under consideration , which defines harassment in a way that captures the type of abusive and threatening messages these athletes routinely receive. The bill goes even further and designates those individuals convicted of harassment and stalking an amateur athlete as a prohibited sports bettor. A federal standard would ensure consistent treatment across jurisdictions.

Additionally, the legislation should allow collegiate athletes to sue individuals who engage in this type of abusive conduct. The ability to recover monetary damages would create a meaningful deterrent. Because much of this behavior is driven by financial frustration tied to lost wagers, attaching a financial penalty to that behavior directly targets the source of the problem.

Critics may attempt to mount free speech objections, but this narrowly tailored proposed solution is not aimed at criticism or negative commentary about athletic performance. The legislation would focus on true threats and targeted, repeated harassment toward a student-athlete. The Supreme Court has long recognized that speech made with the intent to threaten or intimidate is not protected under the First Amendment. Essentially, fans should feel free to criticize athletes, but not to terrorize them.

A federal approach would standardize accountability in ways state-by-state systems cannot. Rather than relying on inconsistent banned bettor lists and varying state regulations, national legislation would create a baseline level of protection for collegiate athletes, regardless of where they compete or where the harassment originates.

College athletes accept pressure when they step onto the field. They should not have to accept abuse when they step off it. Moving forward requires more than awareness; it requires accountability. Most importantly, it requires a commitment to protecting the well-being of the athletes who make college sports possible.

Deymon X. Fleming, Jr. is a J.D. candidate at the University of Georgia School of Law.

articles.title: Former Stars and Stripes publisher: Pentagon lawsuit will ‘continue on’ after court setback
articles.summary: Max Lederer, the former longtime publisher of the Stars and Stripes, on Saturday said he and the two other staffers fired by the Pentagon last month will “continue on” in their lawsuit after a federal judge denied their emergency request this week. Lederer and the paper’s former editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte sued…
articles.body:
Max Lederer, the former longtime publisher of the Stars and Stripes, on Saturday said he and the two other staffers fired by the Pentagon last month will “continue on” in their lawsuit after a federal judge denied their emergency request this week.

Lederer and the paper’s former editor-in-chief, Erik Slavin, and reporter Lara Korte sued the Pentagon last week , alleging the department’s decision to dismiss them from their roles violated its own personnel rules and their First Amendment rights.

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden ruled Friday that the employees were not likely to succeed in their claim that these terminations violated their First Amendment rights.

Lederer told MS NOW’s Jacob Soboroff on Saturday morning that this request was only the “first step in the process,” noting that “it’s a really high bar in a preliminary injunction” and that McFadden’s ruling “doesn’t eliminate our basic suit.”

“We are going on with that suit,” he said. “That will continue on, and we’ll have more opportunity to present our case to the judge and argue this very important issue.”

The Pentagon’s leadership under President Trump’s second presidency has attempted to reshape the military outlet’s coverage. Chief Pentagon Spokesperson Sean Parnell said in January that the department would “refocus” the organization’s coverage from “woke distractions that syphon morale.”

While the paper is staffed by members of the Defense Department, the Stars and Stripes has historically enjoyed editorial independence from the Pentagon.

In March, the Pentagon issued an eight-page memo that included a requirement for the paper’s content to be “consistent with good order and discipline of the military.”

Two of the organization’s advisory board members sued the department in June, alleging the Pentagon was attempting to “exert unprecedented control” over the paper and sensor its content.

The department also removed the outlet’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, whose job was to monitor the newspaper’s editorial independence. Smith sued the Pentagon in June over this decision.

Prior to his firing, Lederer had announced his retirement and planned to step down from his role overseeing the paper at the end of this month. He told MS NOW on Saturday that he made this decision after declining Pentagon officials’ request to fire two outlet staffers.

“I had gotten to a point where I couldn’t support the direction any longer, and as any good employee of any good organization, your option is to do what you’re asked to do or leave,” Lederer said. “And I chose to leave.”

articles.title: Democratic lawmakers erupt after anti-Israel journalist calls Hakeem Jeffries an ‘AIPAC monkey’ in viral rant
articles.summary: Rula Jebreal's "AIPAC monkey" remark about Hakeem Jeffries sparked swift backlash from the Congressional Black Caucus and Democratic lawmakers.
articles.body: Anti-Israel journalist Rula Jebreal apologized "unconditionally" after calling House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., an "AIPAC monkey" during an interview earlier this week, a remark the Congressional Black Caucus and several Democratic lawmakers condemned as blatantly racist. The comment came as Jebreal appeared on Wajahat Ali’s "The Left Hook" podcast on Wednesday, where she accused Jeffries — who is Black — of carrying out the agenda of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) and blasted his support for Israel. "His name is Hakeem. ‘Hakeem’ is an Arabic name which means ‘healer.’ He’s not a healer, he’s a divider," Jebreal said. LEFT-WING PODCASTER BLASTS SCHUMER, JEFFRIES AS 'FASCIST COLLABORATORS' "He is a bought and paid by AIPAC monkey," she added. "With all due respect — and I don’t mean it in a racist way." Jebreal continued, "He is just basically an errand boy, and we’re done and tired." Immediately following Jebreal’s comments, host Ali sought to clarify the meaning behind her remarks. "I know you corrected yourself, Rula, but I just want to address it," Ali said. "Using monkey to anyone Black, it has terrible racial connotations. But I think you caught yourself and said you didn’t mean it with any racial animosity." "I didn’t," Jebreal replied. "There’s these three monkeys — one, I cannot hear, I cannot see, I cannot speak – it reminds me of these three monkeys." However, the Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) rejected Jebreal’s explanation of her controversial comments, with other Democratic leaders following suit. "To be clear, there isn’t a non-racist way to call Leader Jeffries — a Black man — a ‘monkey’ or ‘errand boy,’" the group said in a statement posted to X. SOME DEMOCRATS PRIVATELY DISGUSTED BY HASAN PIKER BUT ARE AFRAID TO PUBLICLY CRITICIZE HIM, HOUSE DEM CLAIMS The CBC then pointed to Ali, the podcast’s host and a staunch critic of Israel, adding, "This is what happens when we hold ourselves to such low standards for what’s allowable in our discourse — people get comfortable being openly bigoted." "We have to stop platforming and trafficking in anti-Black racism, whether it’s on the political right or the left," the group concluded. DEM SENATE CANDIDATE MAKES STUNNING ADMISSION ABOUT ANTISEMITISM IN HER PARTY: 'DANGEROUS' Her comments also drew criticism from several Democratic lawmakers, who took to X to condemn the inflammatory statement. "Blatantly racist and offensive rhetoric — it should be condemned by everyone, across the political spectrum. Period," Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo, posted online. DEMOCRATS CONDEMNING HASAN PIKER AS BACKLASH SPREADS THROUGH PARTY Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y., echoed the same sentiment, posting, "Calling a Black man a ‘monkey’ is racist. Full stop." "If Wajahat Ali and Rula Jebreal were on the far right, no one on the far left would have any trouble condemning them for dehumanizing a Black man in racist terms," he continued. "The silence is deafening." DEMOCRAT RIPS HASAN PIKER AS 'HACK WHO THRIVES ON HATE' OVER HIS WARNING TO AMERICAN JEWS ABOUT ISRAEL After the clip circulated online, Jebreal posted an apology to X. "I am disgusted and horrified that Hakeem Jeffries is taking money from AIPAC amidst Israel's genocide in Palestine," Jebreal wrote. "That said, a term that I used to describe him was inappropriate and offensive and should never have been used. I apologize unconditionally." However, Jebreal's attempts at damage control drew a skeptical read from CEO of Axia Public Relations CEO Jason Mudd. "She reasserts the accusation first and tucks the apology at the end. That's not confessing, that's a closing argument with ‘sorry’ bolted on," Mudd told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "The podcast clarification and the written apology target two different audiences: one tried to survive the moment live, the other tried to survive the headline," he continued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Jebreal and Jeffries did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.

articles.title: Judge allows 'homewrecker' lawsuit against former Sen Kyrsten Sinema to move forward
articles.summary: Former U.S. Sen. Kyrsten Sinema can be sued under North Carolina's alienation of affection law after a judge ruled her messages establish jurisdiction.
articles.body: Former U.S. Sen. Kyrsten Sinema can be sued under North Carolina's so-called "homewrecker" law after a federal judge ruled the state has jurisdiction over allegations she helped break up a marriage by having an affair with a woman's then-husband. Sinema acknowledged having a sexual relationship with Matthew Ammel, who was a member of her security detail while she was a senator, but said she could not be sued in North Carolina because she lacks a meaningful connection to the state. U.S. District Judge David A. Bragdon rejected that argument and denied Sinema's motion to dismiss the case, saying she knew Ammel lived in the state with his wife, Heather Ammel, and their three children. Bragdon also pointed out that Heather Ammel discovered the affair in early 2024 after reading nine messages Sinema sent to her then-husband while he was in North Carolina. He found that those communications were enough for Heather Ammel's lawsuit to move forward in the state. JONATHAN TURLEY: FORMER SEN KYRSTEN SINEMA FIGHTS AFFAIR LAWSUIT INVOKING CENTURIES-OLD MARRIAGE TORT In her civil complaint, Heather Ammel is seeking damages from Sinema, claiming the ex-lawmaker interfered with what she described as a "good and loving marriage" by pursuing her then-husband. North Carolina is among the few states that recognize alienation-of-affection claims, allowing spouses to seek damages from a third party they believe caused the breakdown of their marriage. Sinema's lawyers, Steven Epstein and Abigail Jenkins, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In his ruling, the judge found that the messages between the two affair partners showed Sinema was "furthering a romantic relationship" with Ammel and "invading" his marriage both while she went on trips with him and when he was home. SPURNED SPOUSES CASH IN AS NORTH CAROLINA’S 'HOMEWRECKER' LAW TURNS CHEATING INTO A COURTROOM JACKPOT According to Heather Ammel's lawsuit, her husband joined Sinema's security team in 2022 after retiring from the U.S. Army. He then began traveling with her domestically and internationally. Sinema, who is unmarried, said in a July 31 deposition that she first had sex with Ammel around Memorial Day 2024. "We were staying at an Airbnb in Napa, California. We were outside. Matt kissed me. We went inside and had sex," Sinema said in her deposition, which took place at a law office in Raleigh. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP That summer, Ammel stopped wearing his wedding ring and was given a job as a national security fellow in Sinema's Senate office, according to Heather Ammel's lawsuit. Sinema, who represented Arizona in the U.S. House and later in the Senate, said in her deposition she had sexual encounters with Ammel in New York, Washington, Colorado and Arizona, but never North Carolina. The Ammels separated on Nov. 1, 2024, and their divorce was finalized in March 2026, according to court records.

articles.title: Trump-aligned super PAC to spend $10 million in Texas Senate race
articles.summary: MAGA Inc., the super PAC aligned with President Donald Trump, plans to spend $10 million dollars in the Texas Senate race, according to a report filed with the FEC.
articles.body: The Donald Trump-aligned MAGA Inc. super PAC plans to spend millions of dollars in the Texas Senate race, according to a report filed with the Federal Election Commission on Saturday. The group is spending $10 million on TV and digital ads in the race, with the filing suggesting that MAGA Inc. will launch ads targeting state Rep. James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in the Lone Star State. The new spending comes as Republicans call on Trump’s deep-pocketed political operation to engage in the midterms, particularly in this Texas race, where state Attorney General Ken Paxton won the GOP primary against GOP Sen. John Cornyn earlier this year after Trump endorsed Paxton over the sitting senator. Following that endorsement, some of Cornyn’s Senate GOP colleagues have publicly worried that Paxton could have a harder time winning the general election than Cornyn because of several past controversies. Paxton was impeached by the Republican-led state House in 2023 on allegations of bribery and abuse of public trust, though he was later acquitted by the state Senate after a trial. Last year, Paxton’s wife, state Sen. Angela Paxton, announced that she had filed for divorce from the attorney general “on biblical grounds ... in light of recent discoveries,” but declined to share more about her reasoning. Both events have left a sour taste in some Texas Republicans’ mouths about Paxton and his ability to win a statewide general election, particularly this year, as Republicans hope to hold on to their majorities in the House and Senate. Earlier this week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., implored Trump’s team to spend in Texas, where Thune estimated advertising costs $8 million a week. “Their resources need to be brought to bear on Texas because it’s not one that we can lose if we’re going to hang on to a Republican majority,” Thune said this week on Fox News. The majority leader’s comments came as some Republicans who are focused on holding the House and Senate this fall have become frustrated with the president’s lack of engagement in midterm campaigning, four people involved in GOP strategy told NBC News. “Somewhere in him, President Trump knows he should care about the midterms and the success of the party,” one of the people said. “But because of that, it’s too early to tell whether he did enough to help.” Specifically, Republicans have pressed the president to spend part of his MAGA Inc. war chest on Senate races as early as possible, particularly in Texas. “The president said he’s going to campaign and he’s going to spend money,” a GOP operative involved in midterm campaigns told NBC News. “Time will tell if he was wrong to wait this long.” On Wednesday, Trump pledged to travel and support GOP candidates, including Paxton, across the country ahead of November’s midterm elections. “We’re going to go to Texas and work for Ken Paxton, who’s a great guy,” the president told reporters. He also addressed his recent criticism of Paxton’s wardrobe, adding: “You might not like the way he looks. You might not love his look. You might not love his television interviews, but he was the best attorney general in the country ... and that speaks a lot louder than the suit he’s wearing that doesn’t look so great.” MAGA Inc. had more than $400 million in the bank as of July 31, according to the group’s most recent fundraising report. The group began rolling out national TV ads highlighting Trump’s agenda earlier this week. Speaking to reporters Friday, the president said he planned to use MAGA Inc.’s war chest to spend up to $500 million boosting Republican candidates in the midterm elections. “I think I have, like, close to a billion dollars in the super PAC, and I’m allocating probably $400 or $500 million. So I’ll be spending, we’ll be spending,” he said. “I’m going to be making contributions to various campaigns of people that I think are good, Republicans that I think are good,” Trump added later. “People that I think are going to win and can win or are close to winning ... I’m going to spend whatever amount of money necessary to try and help us.”

articles.title: Texas Republican: ‘I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy’
articles.summary: Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial, rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children. “I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy,” Gill said Friday on Fox News’s “The…
articles.body:
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) said he has no sympathy for Lindsay Clancy after her murder trial ended in a mistrial , rejecting the defense’s argument that severe mental illness left her not criminally responsible for killing her three children.

“I don’t have an ounce of sympathy for Lindsay Clancy,” Gill said Friday on Fox News’s “The Will Cain Show.”

“I have an enormous amount of sympathy for the three little innocent kids who were slaughtered,” he said earlier.

Gill went on to push back against the central argument of Clancy’s defense: that she was experiencing postpartum psychosis when she strangled her three children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — at the family’s Massachusetts home in 2023.

“You don’t get licensed to murder your children or anybody else just because you have mental health problems,” Gill said. “We’ve gotten in a habit of medicalizing evil.”

Trial Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial when jurors remained deadlocked for seven days without being able to reach a unanimous verdict on whether Clancy was criminally responsible for the killings.

A last-minute attempt was made by Clancy’s attorneys to remove the lone holdout juror, whom they accused of refusing to properly apply the legal standard of reasonable doubt. Sullivan declined to remove the juror.

The legal battle has dominated national headlines, with even President Trump weighing in to respond to news of the mistrial.

“It’s a shame. It’s a horrible tragedy,” Trump said when asked about the case during an executive order signing ceremony in the Oval Office. “She did a horrible, horrible thing.”

“I guess they’re going to go through another trial. It’s too bad,” he concluded.

articles.title: Trump shakes up RNC midterm convention schedule, says he’ll speak on night one
articles.summary: President Trump is set to speak on Night 1 of the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9. “The Greatest RALLY of them all,” Trump wrote in a Friday Truth Social post. “I’ll be speaking on night one, and hanging around for an earlier closing, and lots of music, on night…
articles.body:
President Trump is set to speak on Night 1 of the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) Midterm Convention in Dallas on Sept. 9.

“The Greatest RALLY of them all,” Trump wrote in a Friday Truth Social post. “I’ll be speaking on night one, and hanging around for an earlier closing, and lots of music, on night two!!! See you in Dallas.”

Vice President J.D. Vance was originally scheduled to deliver the keynote address for night one, with President Trump capping off night two. It’s unclear how the president’s announcement will affect the previously announced schedule.

Trump had previously hinted in an August statement that he would “be with you both nights.”

The first-of-its-kind convention is expected to have Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.), House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is running for Senate in the Lone Star State, in attendance.

Other Republican politicians stated they could not attend – including Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Ala.) saying he could no longer attend as campaign events were added to his schedule and Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) instead meeting with constituents that weekend, according to Newsweek .

The convention shakeup comes as a GOP operative tells the Hill that while Trump has been touting the event for a year, because it was only announced in late June, candidates and incumbents have not been given nearly as much time to plan their participation.

“Lot of things made this very hasty that didn’t need to happen,” the operative said.

Some House members are opting to not attend the convention due to a reported $25,000 in minimum expected contributions, with the highest tier asking for $100,000.

The programming for the event lists over 100 items the RNC will cover such as “Education & Parental Rights” and a panel of Republican candidates campaigning in swing districts across the country.

The RNC will also be “honoring Charlie Kirk’s impact on American youth and converting that legacy into a call to mobilize voters,” on the same day that the political commentator was killed a year ago.

articles.title: Sunday shows preview: Trump travels to Texas for RNC midterm convention; Administration downplays Iran war consequences
articles.summary: President Trump will head to the GOP’s convention in Dallas next week — an event aimed at galvanizing Republican voters to get out the vote ahead of the midterm elections this November. The president will headline the two-day convention, and Vice President JD Vance is also expected to address attendees. Ahead of the inaugural event,…
articles.body:
President Trump will head to the GOP’s convention in Dallas next week — an event aimed at galvanizing Republican voters to get out the vote ahead of the midterm elections this November.

The president will headline the two-day convention, and Vice President JD Vance is also expected to address attendees.

Ahead of the inaugural event, Trump-affiliated super PAC MAGA Inc. gave $10 million to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) campaign — placating some Republicans calls for the president to invest in GOP candidates locked in toss-up races with Democratic challengers.

Trump said yesterday the PAC has $1 billion at its disposal, though reports from June estimated its finances at around $400 million . He added that MAGA Inc. plans to spend between $400 and $500 million for November’s midterms, saving the rest for the 2028 election cycle.

The convention comes amid rising frustration among voters with the president’s handling of the economy and the Iran war.

The Trump administration has attempted to calm concerns about the monthslong conflict, with Vice President Vance telling reporters this week he “wouldn’t call it a war.”

House Republican Conference Chair Rep. Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) will join CBS News’s “Face the Nation” on Sunday, likely set to discuss how Republicans are approaching the November elections.

In a bid to bring down rising U.S. fuel costs tied to global energy shortages during the Iran war, last week the president announced a new deal with Venezuela to gain “majority U.S. control” of a large portion of the country’s massive oil reserves.

Trump’s economic approval rating has taken a hit , as gas prices have hit record highs . This new agreement gives the U.S. a 55 percent “effective output” in 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven reserves, but experts told The Hill it could be a while before this move impacts U.S. gas prices.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright, who has championed this new deal, will appear on several Sunday shows, including “Face the Nation,” CNN’s “State of the Union,” Fox News’s “Fox News Sunday” and ABC News’s “This Week.”

Additionally, the president signed several executive orders this week aimed at bringing down beef costs for American consumers, including a controversial directive to lower high tariffs on imported beef products from countries like Brazil and Argentina.

Ranchers, farmers and some Republican lawmakers have balked at the move, saying it would negatively impact the sale of domestic beef, since these imported goods would be sold at 25 percent under market price.

The U.S. will pause “out-of-quota” tariffs on up to 300,000 metric tons of beef for a 90 – day period in an effort to bring down costs and allow the U.S. cattle population to regrow.

The president sought to address these concerns by adding a new requirement for foreign beef to be labeled with its country-of-origin and allowing American ranchers to process their own meat. The Friday order also asked the Interior Department to consider stripping the grey wolf , a livestock predator, of its endangered species protections.

A day later, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in an attempt to reopen peace negotiations and end its yearslong war with Ukraine. The pair will then travel to Kyiv to talk with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday.

Sen. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.), a senior member of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, will join Fox News’s “Sunday Morning Futures” this weekend . .

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll’s announced resignation on Monday marked the latest departure from the Pentagon under Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Hegseth, who has faced mounting scrutiny for his attempts to impose his will on the service branch, is reportedly considering Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell to replace Driscoll, sources told The Hill.

Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.), a member of the House Committee on Armed Services, called this week for Trump to fire Hegseth. The Democrat will join The Hill’s “The Hill Sunday” this weekend.

The Pentagon’s leadership has also come under fire for its attempts to reshape the Stars and Stripes.

Three of the military outlet’s staffers sued the department last week after they were fired amid Pentagon leadership’s effort to crack down on “woke” coverage. On Friday, a federal judge on Friday denied their request to stop these terminations.

Former Stars and Stripes publisher, Max Lederer, told MS NOW on Saturday morning that he and the two other fired staffers will continue their lawsuit against the department, noting the emergency injunction was only the “first step in the process.”

In another legal battle, Missouri asked the Supreme Court late Friday to restore a congressional map that favors Republicans after a lower court ruled earlier in the week it could not be used in the midterm elections.

In Maryland, the state’s highest court ruled in favor of keeping a Democrat-drawn redistricting referendum on the ballot. If approved, this measure would grant the state’s General Assembly the authority to give the Maryland Supreme Court “original jurisdiction” over congressional redistricting plans, which would likely make it easier for Democrats to win seats.

Maryland Rep. Jamie Raskin (D) will join NBC News’s “Meet the Press” on Sunday.

articles.title: Kennedy Center renews call for Trump-backed shutdown after part of a ceiling collapses
articles.summary: A chunk of ceiling fell inside a main hallway of the Kennedy Center, according to a spokesperson who said the damage underscores the need to shut down the historic arts venue for renovations sought by President Donald Trump.
articles.body: A chunk of ceiling fell inside a main hallway of the Kennedy Center, according to a spokesperson who said the damage underscores the need to shut down the historic arts venue for renovations sought by President Donald Trump. No one was injured when a piece of the ceiling inside the Kennedy Center’s grand foyer collapsed Friday evening, said Roma Daravi, the center’s vice president for public relations. Photos provided by the center showed a large hole in the high ceiling and debris littering the red carpet in part of the hallway that connects the Kennedy Center’s three main performance auditoriums. The damage occurred during stormy weather in Washington. The Kennedy Center’s Trump-aligned board is fighting in court to move forward with plans to add Trump’s name to the building’s facade and to close the center for two years as it undergoes $250 million in renovations. Daravi called the partial ceiling collapse Friday “another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed.” “This structural failure stems from decades of neglect and deferred maintenance by the previous leadership, and there’s no justification for further delays in restoring America’s cultural center,” Daravi said in a statement. Trump’s efforts to add his name and make other big changes to the center established to honor President John F. Kennedy following his assassination are just part of Trump’s broader second-term agenda to reshape Washington. Trump already has demolished the East Wing of the White House to make way for a ballroom. He also plans a triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and a renovated golf course along the Potomac River. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper ruled in May that Trump’s name had been added to the Kennedy Center illegally and ordered that it be taken down. He also blocked the administration from closing the venue for renovations. Now before the judge is an August vote by the Kennedy Center’s board to return Trump’s name to the facade so reads: “The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump.” Justice Department lawyers have argued donations for renovations will dry up without Trump’s name on the building. Other changes have moved forward. Last week, the Kennedy Center took down a large stick figure sculpture known as Blue that had stood outside the center in 2019. The Kennedy Center gave no reason for its removal, but said in a statement “we are honored to have been stewards” of the late sculptor Joel Shapiro’s work. Grace Terpstra of Keep the KC, a community group fighting the Kennedy Center’s closure, said she suspects the board will seize on what appears to be limited ceiling damage “to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down, that it’s going to fall on everybody.” “I think they’ll try to make it into a bigger thing and show that they’ve found a lot of other things,” said Terpstra, the group’s founder.

articles.title: North Carolina Dem Senate candidate added former Bloods gang member to criminal justice task force: report
articles.summary: Roy Cooper appointed a convicted Bloods gang member to his criminal justice reform task force in 2020, a Washington Free Beacon report reveals.
articles.body: Roy Cooper, the former Democrat governor of North Carolina now running for Senate, added an ex-member of the notorious Bloods gang to a "Racial Equity in Criminal Justice" task force in 2020. In the wake of George Floyd's 2020 death, Cooper created the task force via executive order, The Washington Free Beacon reported. Cooper, who tapped then state attorney general turned current Gov. Josh Stein to lead the task force, stocked the panel with a mix of state officials and community activists, including Kerwin Pittman, who was convicted in 2007 of conspiracy to commit murder, serving 14 years in prison for the crime, according to records obtained by the Free Beacon. Pittman was also identified as a "ranking member of the Bloods" by prosecutors during a murder trial for Bloods member Michael Contrez Jones. SIX-FIGURE PRIVATE SECURITY BILL FOR TOP DEM SENATE HOPEFUL FUELS GOP HYPOCRISY CLAIMS Pittman was convicted in connection to the 2006 drive-by-shooting of 19-year-old Jamel Amiens Jeffreys, the Free Beacon reported. Pittman defended his involvement in the task force and argued his past actions were the result of poor judgment as a teenager. "I was asked to contribute to conversations about criminal justice reform because of both my lived experience and the work I was doing in communities," Pittman told the Free Beacon. "I have never hidden my past. The gang involvement and criminal conduct you reference occurred when I was a teenager and young man, at or before the age of 19. I am now 39 years old." ONE YEAR AFTER IRYNA ZARUTSKA MURDER, VIOLENT CRIMES FUEL NORTH CAROLINA PUBLIC SAFETY DEBATE "I made decisions as a young person that had serious consequences, including spending more than a decade incarcerated," he added. Pittman, according to his LinkedIn profile, worked at the time of the task force's creation for Emancipate NC, an organization which, as the Free Beacon reported, has often called for the abolition of police, writing that "maintaining white supremacy has always been the goal of policing," in a 2023 company blog post. Cooper, who is running for Senate against former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley, referenced his opponent's record when asked to comment on the Free Beacon story. DEM SENATE HOPEFUL PIVOTS ON DATA CENTERS AS RISING POWER COSTS COLLIDE WITH CAMPAIGN "While Roy spent his career putting rapists and violent criminals behind bars and signing tough on crime laws as governor, Michael Whatley spent his appointing a convicted child sex predator who served six years in prison and spent over a decade as a registered sex offender to a top role within the North Carolina Republican Party that gave him access to events with children," the Cooper campaign told Fox News Digital in a statement. articles.title: Trump faces down beef backlash. Will import plan pay off?
articles.summary: President Trump is pushing ahead with his plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans, despite the backlash from cattle farmers and Republicans whose states would be most be most affected. In an apparent effort to soften the blow, Trump signed executive orders Friday, including one that allows ranchers and…
articles.body:
President Trump is pushing ahead with his plan to import foreign beef as a way to reduce prices for Americans, despite the backlash from cattle farmers and Republicans whose states would be most be most affected.

In an apparent effort to soften the blow, Trump signed executive orders Friday, including one that allows ranchers and farmers to process and package their own products, and another that promotes country-of-origin labeling across all foreign beef, which would require congressional action.

Justin Tupper, president of the United States Cattlemen’s Association, said it appreciated the new orders but remained “cautious on what comes next.”

Following the signings in the Oval Office, Trump sought to play down the impact of his beef import plan, telling reporters, “We’re doing it in a very limited fashion because our ranchers can handle it,” adding, “Our ranchers want the prices to be down too.”

When announcing the move last month to import 300,000 metric tons of beef without tariffs for 90 days, Trump said the beef would be sold at 25 percent below current market prices. He revealed for the first time Friday the beef would be coming primarily from Brazil and Argentina.

Those critical of the move say it will barely move the needle on Americans’ cost-of-living concerns, while forcing a key part of Trump’s base to pay a heavy price.

“Trump is right to address the issue of beef prices but stepped in it in doing so in a way that parts of his base are going to react to,” said Doug Heye, a longtime GOP strategist.

“The administration — and Trump in particular — need to be spending all their efforts on lowering prices across the board, including the latest cost driver, Iran,” he added.

Glynn Tonsor, an assistant professor in the Kansas State University Department of Agricultural Economics, said the odds of this deal lowering prices and helping ranchers “are about zero.”

“If there’s something that reduces beef prices for consumers, by definition, that reduces the dollars going back into the industry, because the price clearing the market for retail beef is lower, and therefore one has to pause and say, is that good for producers?” he said. “So, there’s a world where one or the other might happen, but I don’t see any world where both could happen out of the same announcement.”

The 300,000 metric ton figure only represents about a 2 percent increase in beef supply, Tonsor noted.

“I’m on record saying it’ll have very, very small, if any, impact on the price that consumers pay for beef,” he said.

Beef prices have been soaring across the country. The average price of 100 percent ground beef per pound in the U.S. is roughly $6.89, according to U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data shared by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis .

The prices have gone up because the U.S. is raising record-low cattle numbers due to several factors, including droughts and rising operational costs, all the while demand remains high.

Data from the Department of Agriculture showed that the U.S started with 86.2 million cattle at the beginning of the year, the lowest cattle inventory since 1951 .

Affordability, meanwhile, remains a top issue for voters ahead of the midterms. Trump captured 62 percent of the rural vote in 2024, but his approval among that voter group has fallen from July to August, according to polls done by ActiVote .

The cattle industry and GOP lawmakers argue that lowering prices for Americans shouldn’t come at the cost of America’s ranchers.

“While America’s cattle producers share the goal of keeping groceries affordable for consumers, flooding the market with government-subsidized, below-market beef is not the way to rebuild the American cattle herd,” Colin Woodall, CEO of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, said in a statement.

“This is a critical time of year for cattle producers, as we approach the season where they are making decisions regarding their herds,” he added, saying the import plan throws “cold water” on the investment necessary to expand herds.

David Anderson, a professor and extension specialist in livestock and food product marketing at Texas A&M University, said the markets should have been left to work themselves out.

“You have to have cattle producers that are profitable to get that market signal to expand, to increase beef production which then brings down prices,” Anderson said. “And so, we finally have prices that are profitable and something like this gets announced.”

He said it comes at a bad time when ranchers are making decisions about their herds.

“This was just another announcement, another thing hitting the market to drive down prices,” he said. “Lowering prices reduces that incentive to expand.”

Several Republican lawmakers have spoken out too. Sens. Chuck Grassley (Iowa) and Jerry Moran (Kan.), Rep. Adrian Smith (Neb.) and 50 others wrote a letter to Trump urging him to prioritize policies that would help ranchers.

“Cattle markets are cyclical, and ranchers use the upswings to prepare for the inevitable downturn,” the lawmakers wrote. “Any intervention in the natural system, especially at a time when producers are making marketing decisions, threatens to pick winners and losers and undermine the long-term viability of family-owned cattle operations throughout the supply chain.”

A report from The Wall Street Journal earlier this past week said that Trump met with Joesley Batista, who shares control of JBS, the world’s largest meatpacker, in the Oval Office a day before he made the announcement.

The sources said that during the meeting, Batista lobbied Trump to drop the import tax as a way to mitigate costs of beef for consumers.

In response to the report, the White House said Trump’s “action to address a short-term supply crunch in the beef market was the result of a long policy planning and coordination process involving domestic stakeholders; this action was not done as the result of any one conversation.”

Brandon Scholz, a former Republican turned independent political analyst from Wisconsin, said Trump’s move gives a “false sense of hope to consumers … and then we’re going to start losing our producers and our growers.”

“I think he’s just putting out a false sense of security in front of the midterms,” Scholz said. “I simply can’t imagine that this is something that people are going to go to the voting booth and go, ‘You know, that was really great that Trump got us all that cheap beef.’”

articles.title: Trump’s MAGA Inc. super-PAC funnels $10 million into Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign
articles.summary: President Trump’s super-PAC MAGA Inc. gave $10 million to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published Saturday. The $10 million payment, given to political media company, Del Ray Media, funded two attack ads against his Democratic opponent James Talarico —…
articles.body:
President Trump’s super-PAC MAGA Inc. gave $10 million to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton’s (R) Senate campaign ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings published Saturday.

The $10 million payment , given to political media company, Del Ray Media, funded two attack ads against his Democratic opponent James Talarico — who is running a surprisingly competitive race in the historically red Lone Star State.

A MAGA Inc. spokesperson, Alex Pfeiffer, told The Hill the MAGA Inc.-funded ads focus on how “High Tax Talarico” is planning to “take money out of Texans’ pockets.”

“MAGA Inc. is going to ensure Texas knows about Talarico’s radical policies and elects Ken Paxton to the U.S. Senate,” Pfeiffer said in her Saturday statement.

Talarico has made promises to put a higher tax on billionaires while cutting taxes for working families and small businesses, while Paxton has advocated for tax breaks and tackling the ongoing affordability crisis.

The Lone Star Liberty PAC is slated to run similar attack ads against Talarico in September for being sympathetic to China, as the current state representative voted against legislation last year establishing criminal penalties for foreign entities purchasing Texas land.

The spending comes after Republican strategist Karl Rove said Wednesday that the “time is running out” for Paxton, who some polls have placed behind his opponent.

“Of the president wants to have Paxton win, he needs to be tossing a lot of money Paxton’s way so that ads can be run that depict Talarico as the far-left winger that he is,” Rove said.

Trump said yesterday the PAC has $1 billion at its disposal amid Republicans’ calls for him to invest further in midterm candidates, though reports from June estimated its finances at around $400 million . He added that MAGA Inc. plans to spend between $400 and $500 million for November’s midterms, saving the rest for the 2028 election cycle.

Paxton pulled ahead in the Republican primary when he earned the president’s endorsement , though he has struggled to build a sustainable lead over his opponent since the primaries

Despite Trump winning the Lone Star state by around 14 points in the 2024 presidential election, Paxton trailed Talarico by 6-points in an August poll from Texas Public Opinion Research .

The Republican has also faced several notable scandals, including the Texas state House voting to impeach him on corruption charges — of which the state senate later acquitted him.

Democrats are increasingly hopeful they can flip Texas’ seat, which Republicans have held for the last three decades. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report also shifted the Texas Senate race to a toss-up — citing Paxton’s high disapproval ratings and “notably underperforming even a generic Republican in GOP polling.”
